entity.name: Epicurus
entity.description: The philosopher who told humanity to stop fearing death. Epicurus founded one of antiquity's most influential schools in an Athenian garden, teaching that atoms and void compose all reality, that gods ignore human affairs, and that pleasure—defined as the absence of pain—is life's highest good. He wrote over 300 works; nearly all are lost.

story.name: Epicurus
story.description: Born on Samos, expelled from Mytilene, founds The Garden in Athens between rival schools, dies in agony yet writes a cheerful final letter. A philosopher's life in the atomic universe.

moments.name: Epicurus Is Born in an Athenian Colony on the Island of Samos
moments.subtitle: The future founder of atomic philosophy arrives seven years after Plato's death
moments.description: In February 341 BCE, Epicurus is born to Athenian parents Neocles and Chaerestrate in the Athenian settlement on Samos, an Aegean island off the coast of modern Turkey. Epicurus grows up during the final years of the Greek Classical Period—Plato has been dead seven years, and Alexander the Great is about to cross into Persia. As a boy, Epicurus studies under the Samian Platonist Pamphilus for roughly four years before military service and exile reshape his path. His birth on a colonial island rather than in Athens itself foreshadows a philosophy that will embrace universal outlook over parochial Greek elitism.

moments.name: Epicurus Is Forced Out of Mytilene After His Teachings Cause Strife
moments.subtitle: A thirty-year-old philosopher's radical ideas prove too dangerous for Lesbos
moments.description: Around 311 BCE, Epicurus begins teaching philosophy in Mytilene on the island of Lesbos at roughly age thirty. His doctrines—that gods ignore human affairs, that atoms and void compose all reality, and that pleasure means the absence of pain—directly contradict the dominant Platonist orthodoxy. The local establishment reacts with hostility, and Epicurus is forced to leave. The expulsion pushes him to found a school in Lampsacus before relocating to Athens. Being driven out of Mytilene becomes the catalyst for The Garden, the school that will spread Epicureanism across the ancient world.

moments.name: Epicurus Founds The Garden in Athens Between Two Rival Schools
moments.subtitle: A commune of philosophers who share meals, welcome women, and reject hierarchy
moments.description: Around 306 BCE, Epicurus purchases a garden in Athens situated halfway between the Stoa and Plato's Academy—his school's two philosophical rivals. The Garden operates as a commune: members hold property in common, share simple meals, and discuss philosophy without hierarchy between teachers and students. Remarkably for the era, The Garden welcomes women as full participants, including Leontion and Themista. The school becomes the institutional base for Epicureanism, which will rival Stoicism for centuries and peak in popularity during the late Roman Republic.

moments.name: Epicurus Proposes That Atoms Randomly Swerve, Giving Humans Free Will
moments.subtitle: A single addition to Democritus's atomic theory rescues human agency from determinism
moments.description: During his decades teaching in Athens, Epicurus develops his modification of Democritus's atomic theory by introducing the concept of the atomic swerve (clinamen). Democritus had argued that all matter consists of atoms moving through void, but this implied a fully deterministic universe. Epicurus adds that atoms occasionally deviate randomly from their downward paths, causing collisions that create the visible world. The swerve also accounts for human free will—without it, every thought and action would be predetermined. This idea anticipates debates about determinism and randomness that persist in physics and philosophy two millennia later.

moments.name: Epicurus Dies in Agony Yet Writes a Cheerful Final Letter
moments.subtitle: The philosopher of pleasure proves his own teachings while dying of kidney stones
moments.description: In 270 BCE, Epicurus dies at age seventy-two in Athens from a stone blockage of his urinary tract after prolonged, severe pain. According to his successor Hermarchus, Epicurus remains cheerful and continues teaching until the end. In what may be his final letter—addressed to his student Idomeneus—Epicurus writes that the cheerfulness of his mind from philosophical contemplation counterbalances his suffering. He asks Idomeneus to care for the children of his late student Metrodorus. The letter is the ultimate test case for Epicurean philosophy: its founder proving that mental tranquility can overcome bodily agony.
